intro: Sleigh bells rattle and the violins begin a comfortable G-major tune. Mahler’s Fourth seems to have wandered into an eighteenth-century drawing room, until its melodies start talking over one another and the trumpets sound an alarm.

cues.title: Bells outside, violins within
cues.text: Flutes chatter above sleigh bells. The violins enter with a little upward flourish and settle into a G-major tune, while the lower strings pluck beneath them. Mahler marks the melody Recht gemächlich — very leisurely.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 4, full score, opening page, printed p. 231: flutes, sleigh bells, violin entry and pizzicato accompaniment. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP70999-PMLP58739-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._4_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rain at Bad Aussee
cues.text: At Bad Aussee in the summer of 1899, poor weather and the resort’s music keep Mahler from composing. His holiday is nearly over when the Fourth begins to come. He works at speed, then finishes the symphony the following summer at Maiernigg.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony guide, work history: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Completion at Maiernigg in August 1900 is documented at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._4_(Mahler)

cues.title: The cellos sing broadly
cues.text: The second tune belongs to the cellos, in D major. Its long notes stretch out after the violins’ little turns and scales. Mahler writes Breit gesungen — broadly sung — over a melody that sounds as though it has all afternoon.
cues.evidence: Basinger describes the cello second theme and Breit gesungen: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Its D-major key is documented in the score and at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._4_(Mahler)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The ending comes first
cues.text: In 1892 Mahler writes Das himmlische Leben, a song about heaven’s food and music. He considers it for the Third Symphony, then makes it the end of the Fourth. These orchestral movements grow towards a song already several years old.
cues.evidence: Basinger dates the song’s piano and orchestral versions to February and March 1892 and traces its changing place in Mahler’s plans: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

cues.title: The bells turn troublesome
cues.text: The opening flute figure returns in the minor, tangled with pieces of the violin tune. Horns make the little descending triplets suddenly forceful. A new flute melody rises from the low strings’ rumbling; it carries a hint of the finale’s song.
cues.evidence: Basinger’s first-movement guide describes the development’s minor-mode opening, horn triplets, low strings and new flute melody: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler explains the connections
cues.text: In 1911 Mahler writes to Georg Göhler: “Each of the three movements is joined thematically with the last one in a most intimate and meaningful way.” The finale’s song is already threading through this orchestra.
cues.evidence: Mahler to Georg Göhler concerning his 1911 essay on the Fourth; the letter is quoted in Basinger’s work history: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

cues.title: The trumpet meets a wall
cues.text: The development’s melody reaches the trumpet in the major. Then a harsh orchestral chord stops its progress. As the tumult clears, trumpets and horns are left sounding military calls across the suddenly empty space.
cues.evidence: Basinger describes the major-mode trumpet melody, dissonant interruption and ensuing trumpet and horn fanfares: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The violin tune returns
cues.text: The first theme comes back quietly in G major, changed in its details. The orchestra soon brightens around it, and the broad cello tune follows. Familiar melodies have survived a decidedly unfamiliar middle.
cues.evidence: Basinger describes the modified first theme, jubilant continuation and return of the second theme in the recapitulation: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A last quick farewell
cues.text: Bits of the first tune keep slipping into the quiet closing melody. They grow into the coda, which gathers itself for a lively ending. The violin tune gets the last word.
cues.evidence: Basinger describes first-theme fragments entering the ruhig closing tune and growing into the coda’s lively conclusion: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: D major opens a longer phrase
transitions.from: A · Sleigh bells and a violin tune
transitions.to: B · The cellos sing in D major
transitions.how: The first theme’s continuation accelerates towards D major, the dominant of G. The cellos then take the melody in long notes, marked Breit gesungen. The violin turns and short scales have led into a lower, more expansive singing line.
transitions.evidence: Basinger’s account of the accelerating transition and cello second theme: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . D-major key: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._4_(Mahler)

transitions.title: The flute figure turns to minor
transitions.from: B · The cellos sing in D major
transitions.how: The exposition settles back into G major and its quiet closing tune. The development reintroduces the opening flute figure in the minor, combining it with pieces of the first theme. The horns seize on the tune’s descending triplets.
transitions.evidence: Basinger, first-movement guide, exposition ending and development opening: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

transitions.title: A dissonance cuts across the trumpet
transitions.to: Dev · Trumpets and the orchestral collision
transitions.how: The development melody clears into the major and reaches the trumpet. A dissonant orchestral chord cuts across it. The massed winds and strings then fall away, exposing military fanfares in trumpets and horns.
transitions.evidence: Basinger describes the trumpet statement, dissonant interruption and fanfare aftermath: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

transitions.title: The fanfares leave room for violins
transitions.from: Dev · Trumpets and the orchestral collision
transitions.to: A′ · The violin tune comes home
transitions.how: The trumpet and horn calls subside. A quiet, altered version of the first theme restores G major in the strings. Its familiar phrase replaces the isolated fanfares, before cymbals announce a more jubilant continuation.
transitions.evidence: Basinger, transition from the fanfares to the recapitulation and its cymbal-led expansion: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

transitions.title: The first tune interrupts its farewell
transitions.from: A′ · The violin tune comes home
transitions.to: Coda · The first tune takes its leave
transitions.how: The quiet closing melody returns in G major with small phrases from the first violin tune tucked inside it. Those fragments keep the music moving into the coda. The orchestra thins before gathering for the quick final bars.
transitions.evidence: Basinger’s account of the ruhig closing theme and first-theme fragments that become the coda: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 4, I. Bedächtig, full score
source.locator: First movement, pp. 231–274, rehearsal figures 1–23: sleigh-bell opening, cello second theme, trumpet outburst and returning violin tune.

timeline.note: Flutes and sleigh bells frame the first violin tune; winds answer its turns and short figures.
Cellos begin the broadly sung second theme; violins continue its long line above soft wind harmony.
Woodwinds trade short phrases above lighter string figures after the broad cello melody.
Bells and flute figures return; horns and divided strings pass fragments through the development.
High wind phrases, horn calls and quick string lines overlap, with harp and percussion between them.
The trumpet melody rises above winds and strings before a harsh orchestral chord interrupts it.
Trumpet and horn fanfares emerge as the strings retreat; soft woodwind figures answer.
The returning violin theme sits over pizzicato inner strings, with horn and wind answers.
The broad lyrical line returns in the strings, supported by wind chords and sustained horns.
Low clarinet figures and quiet strings weave opening fragments into the closing pages; bells briefly return.
Strings and upper winds gather into the quick close; horns, trumpet, timpani, triangle and cymbals reinforce it.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
